explain.say: On 28 June 1919, exactly five years after Sarajevo, German delegates signed a peace treaty in the Hall of Mirrors at Versailles, the very room where the German Empire had been proclaimed in 1871. Look at the sorting board. These are the demands Germany had to accept. Which group looks hardest to swallow?

explain.say: See the timeline. The peace was made in Paris by the winners. France's Georges Clemenceau wanted security and payment for a devastated north; US President Woodrow Wilson wanted his Fourteen Points, self-determination and a League of Nations; Britain's Lloyd George sat between them. Germans called it a Diktat, a dictated peace. Why might that word stick?

explain.say: Now the map. Germany returned Alsace-Lorraine to France and gave land to a new Poland, including a corridor to the sea that split off East Prussia. It lost all its colonies, and the Rhineland was demilitarised. In all Germany lost about 13 percent of its European land and about 10 percent of its people. Which change would anger Germans most?

Article 231 said Germany and its allies were responsible for the war's loss and damage, the so-called war guilt clause, which justified reparations. Look at the sizes, all approximate: the 1921 headline bill was 132 billion gold marks, but only about 50 billion was really expected, and Germany paid about 20 billion before payments ended in 1932. What does that gap suggest?

explain.say: Now the debate. John Maynard Keynes called it a Carthaginian peace that would wreck Europe. Historians like Margaret MacMillan and Sally Marks reply that Germany stayed united and strong, and that the bigger failure was enforcement. Excellent. Exam tip: don't draw a straight line from Versailles to Hitler; the Depression mattered hugely.

faq.q: What were the terms of the Treaty of Versailles?
faq.a: Germany lost Alsace-Lorraine, land to Poland and all its colonies, was limited to an army of 100,000 with no air force or submarines, had to demilitarise the Rhineland, accepted Article 231 on responsibility for the war and had to pay reparations.
asks: What military limits were placed on Germany?

faq.q: Was the Treaty of Versailles too harsh?
faq.a: John Maynard Keynes argued in 1919 that it was a vindictive, economically ruinous peace. Many later historians, such as Margaret MacMillan and Sally Marks, argue it was less harsh than claimed, left Germany united and potentially powerful, and failed mainly because it was not enforced.
asks: What did Keynes say about Versailles?

faq.q: How much did Germany actually pay in reparations?
faq.a: In 1921 the total was set at 132 billion gold marks, but most of that was in bonds never expected to be paid; about 50 billion was the real demand. Germany paid roughly 20 billion gold marks, much of it financed by US loans, before payments ended in 1932.
The clause stating that Germany and its allies were responsible for causing all the loss and damage of the war. Germans called it the war guilt clause and bitterly resented it.
asks: What was the war guilt clause?

faq.a: US President Woodrow Wilson's peace programme of January 1918, including open diplomacy, free trade, arms reduction, self-determination for peoples and a League of Nations. Only parts of it entered the treaty.

facts: The Treaty of Versailles was signed on 28 June 1919 in the Hall of Mirrors.
The German army was limited to 100,000 men.
The US Senate never ratified the Treaty of Versailles.

quiz.say: Germany paid about 20 billion of a 132 billion gold mark headline bill. Roughly what percentage is that?
quiz.why: 20 divided by 132 is about 0.15, so roughly 15 percent.

wrong.2: Ninety percent would be about 119 billion.
